To burrow means to dig a hole or tunnel into the ground — usually by pushing the earth aside with your body, claws, or hands. Picture a rabbit using its front paws to push through soil, moving deeper and deeper underground. That action is called burrowing.

But the word reaches far beyond animals digging in dirt. Over time, "burrow" has grown to describe any movement that resembles digging — where something pushes, wriggles, or squeezes its way into or through something else.

1. The literal sense — actually digging into the ground

This is the most basic use. An animal (or person) physically digs into soil, sand, or another surface.

  • The mole burrowed through the soft earth.
  • The crab burrowed into the wet sand at the beach.

The key idea: something is moving material aside to go deeper and create a passage or a hiding place.

2. Pushing or squeezing into a snug space

You don't have to be digging actual dirt to use "burrow." If something pushes its way into a tight, soft, or enclosed space — the way an animal slides into its hole — we say it burrows.

  • She burrowed under the warm blanket on a cold night. (She pulled herself deep into the covers, snug and hidden, like an animal retreating into its tunnel.)
  • The puppy burrowed into the pile of laundry. (It pushed itself inside the pile until it disappeared.)
  • He burrowed his face into the pillow.

The feeling here is one of going inward — getting warm, hidden, or deeply enclosed inside something soft or sheltering.

3. Moving through something dense or crowded

When a person or thing moves through a crowded or tight space by pushing and squeezing, we use "burrow" to capture that effortful, wriggling movement.

  • She burrowed through the crowd to reach the exit. (She pushed her way through tightly packed people.)
  • The kitten burrowed between the sofa cushions.

Again, the image is similar: moving through something dense, the way an animal pushes through compacted soil.

4. Searching through a pile of things

"Burrow" is also used when someone rummages through a pile — papers, a bag, a drawer — moving things aside to find something, just like an animal moves soil aside.

  • He burrowed through the box of old letters looking for her address.
  • She burrowed around in her handbag until she found her keys.

This sense has a quality of searching with effort, moving things around persistently and with purpose.

5. The figurative sense — going deeply into something mentally

In a more abstract sense, "burrow" can describe going deeply into a subject, a feeling, or a problem — just as an animal goes deeper and deeper underground.

  • She burrowed into her research, spending hours reading every article she could find. (She dove deeply, not staying at the surface.)
  • He let his mind burrow into the problem until he found the answer.
The thread that ties all these senses together

No matter which sense you encounter, "burrow" always carries the same three qualities:

Going inward or deeper — always into something, never across the surface of it. A bird skims across the sky; a mole burrows into the earth. The direction of "burrow" is always inward.

Effort and persistence — burrowing is never casual or effortless. It involves pushing, working, or squeezing your way through something that offers some resistance — soil, a crowd, a pile of papers, a difficult subject.

A sense of purpose — animals burrow to hide from danger, to build a home, or to find food. Humans burrow under blankets for warmth and comfort. People burrow through papers to find something specific. There is almost always a reason driving the burrowing.

"Burrow" almost always appears with a preposition that tells you where or into what the burrowing happens. Knowing these will help you recognise and use the word correctly in any context:

  • burrow into — She burrowed into her work / the soft pillow / the research.
  • burrow through — He burrowed through the crowd / the files / the undergrowth.
  • burrow under — The dog burrowed under the fence / the blanket.
  • burrow between — The mouse burrowed between the walls.

"Burrow" is an ordinary, everyday word — not formal, not slang. It works naturally in both spoken and written English. It has a vivid, physical quality to it: when someone uses it, you almost immediately see the action — something pressing inward, pushing through, disappearing into. That vividness is what makes it such a satisfying and precise word to use.
